name: gmt
desc: Tools for manipulating and plotting geographic and Cartesian data
why: Mature geoscience toolkit for plotting maps and data; real science you can run at home, though well known in its field.

brief.what_it_is: GMT (Generic Mapping Tools) is an open source collection of about 100 command-line tools for manipulating geographic and Cartesian data sets, including filtering, trend fitting, gridding and projecting. It takes in tabular or gridded data and produces high-quality illustrations, from simple x-y plots and contour maps to artificially illuminated surfaces, 3D perspective views and animations. GMT supplements add about 50 more specialized tools, and it supports over 30 map projections. It can also be called from MATLAB/Octave, Julia, Python, C and C++ through wrapper libraries.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames GMT as a free, open source toolbox for Earth, ocean and planetary science that lets researchers process data and produce publication-quality illustrations, automate workflows and make animations. The README adds that it is used well beyond geoscience, in medical research, engineering, physics, government and hobbyist work.
brief.how_it_works: GMT is a set of command-line programs that are chained together in scripts to read data, transform it and draw the result. The README says GMT requires support data such as GSHHG coastlines, rivers and political boundaries, and optionally DCW country polygons. Since GMT 6 it has also been rebuilt as an API that the language wrappers call.
brief.install_notes: The README lists three tar archives: gmt-6.x.x.tar.gz (the GMT 6 distribution), gshhg-gmt-2.x.x.tar.gz (all five resolutions of GSHHG coastline data, needed) and dcw-gmt-2.x.x.tar.gz (Digital Chart of the World polygons, optional). Separate installers exist for macOS and Windows. The README says it installs on UNIX, Linux, macOS, FreeBSD and OpenBSD, and also on Windows, Cygwin and virtual machines. It points to install instructions at docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/latest/install.html and build-from-source instructions in BUILDING.md. The Homebrew caveats say psconvert needs Ghostscript, movie needs FFmpeg for MP4/WebM and GraphicsMagick for animated GIF, and these must be installed separately. I did not fetch the install docs, so I have no first-run steps.
brief.standout: GMT has been around for decades and is used in many published figures, yet it is free and LGPL-licensed. It is now also a callable API with wrappers for Python (PyGMT), Julia and MATLAB/Octave, so it can sit inside modern analysis code as well as in shell scripts. The README also lists colour maps from several sources, including Scientific Colour Maps, cmocean and cpt-city.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage news includes an entry dated 2026-07-15 announcing the first PyGMT paper, and the README copyright runs to 1991-2026. The homepage's 'Latest releases' section showed no version number, so I did not confirm a release date.
brief.caveats: The README says the project is open source with no paid support. It asks users to report bugs through GitHub issues and questions to the community forum. Licensed under LGPL v3 or later. Building from source is documented but I did not check its difficulty. Movie and psconvert features depend on external tools (Ghostscript, FFmpeg, GraphicsMagick) that the Homebrew caveats say must be installed separately. Coastline and other support data must be downloaded for maps to draw. The Homebrew formula's caveats mention a movie command and a psconvert command, but these appear only in the Homebrew text, not in the README I read.

judge.reason: An extensive command-line geoscience toolkit that transforms spatial data into maps, grids, and illuminated 3D surfaces offers a substantial scientific rabbit hole.

entry.title: GMT (Generic Mapping Tools)
entry.tldr: About 100 command-line tools that turn tables and grids of data into publication-quality maps, contour plots, 3D views and animations.
entry.deeper_look:
GMT is a collection of command-line programs for geographic and Cartesian data. Some filter, fit trends, grid and project data. Others draw the result: x-y plots, contour maps, artificially illuminated surfaces, 3D perspective views and animations. It supports more than 30 map projections, and supplements add roughly 50 more specialised tools.

The homepage calls it "A toolbox for Earth, Ocean, and Planetary Science". It exists so researchers can process data and produce figures in scripts, then rerun the same script when the data changes. The README says it is also used in medical research, engineering, physics, government and hobbyist work.

The underlying idea is that a map is the output of a pipeline. You chain small programs in a shell script: read data, transform it, draw it. Since GMT 6 the same machinery is also an API, and wrappers let you call it from Python (PyGMT), Julia, MATLAB/Octave, C and C++. The project dates back to 1991 and appears in a great many published figures.

The README says GMT needs support data, namely GSHHG coastlines, rivers and political boundaries, plus optional DCW country polygons. That is part of the setup, so expect to look at the install docs before your first map.
entry.install:
brew install gmt
# optional, per the Homebrew caveats:
brew install ghostscript      # needed for psconvert (PostScript to other formats)
brew install ffmpeg           # needed for movie, for MP4/WebM
brew install graphicsmagick   # needed for movie, for animated GIFs
# GMT also needs GSHHG coastline data to draw maps; see the install docs.
